items.title: Had a look at Cordis, the theory behind DeepSeek Harness's plugin architecture. Quick thoughts:
items.author: Zhengyao Jiang
items.content_text:
Had a look at Cordis, the theory behind DeepSeek Harness's plugin architecture. Quick thoughts:

It's basically a theory that, as long as you follow a set of contracts for the components of a harness, there are theoretical guarantees that your harness can safely remove a component.

It can potentially be powerful, especially when you have a gigantic harness that is self-evolved. The agent might do some real-time experiments, sort of like A/B testing: adding a new component, and if that component isn't useful, reverting it. In this framework, as long as you know the contracts are followed, you don't have to reason through the complex global dependencies to figure out how or if you can safely revert it.

The main limitation though, is that those constraints aren't very easy to follow precisely in practice, especially with an LLM involved.

For example, constraints like module independence and acyclicity are easier to reason about in a purely programmatic setting. However, once the harness has an LLM in the loop, the LLM context window naturally introduces really complex dependencies. Essentially, everything can end up depending on everything else.

The framework ofc might still be powerful for designing harnesses, something like React for harnesses. To me, it depends on to what extent the empirical robustness benefits still hold despite the contracts not being followed exactly, versus the additional work introduced by trying to follow those contracts.

Either way, I think it's super exciting that there are more and more attempts to treat harness design as a serious science instead of a collection of ad hoc tricks. Very bullish on the direction of mathematically grounded harness design in general.

items.title: DeepSeek just open-sourced DeepSeek Harness v0.1, a modular framework for building AI agents where virtually every part of the agent stack is replaceable as a plugin.
items.author: Wes Roth
items.content_text:
DeepSeek just open-sourced DeepSeek Harness v0.1, a modular framework for building AI agents where virtually every part of the agent stack is replaceable as a plugin.

Instead of hard-wiring the model, tools, memory, sandbox, filesystem, orchestration, agent loop, or UI into one framework, DeepSeek Harness lets developers swap and extend those components independently. Even the model adapter, tool registry, session log, and agent loop are plugins rather than a privileged core.

It's MIT-licensed, available now on GitHub, and can be launched through npm with npx  deepseek-ai/dsh web. DeepSeek also ships both web and headless configurations.

items.title: Small tip for anyone trying DeepSeek Harness (DSH) GUI: it opened in Chinese for me.
items.author: Elliot 艾略特
items.content_text:
Small tip for anyone trying DeepSeek Harness (DSH) GUI: it opened in Chinese for me. 

Here’s the 6-second way to switch it to English.

While exploring it, I found something much more interesting:

“Everything is a plugin” is only the surface. 

DSH has opt-in tools that let an agent inspect its own runtime, define a plugin, run it, and stop it. 

When the plugin stops, Cordis unwinds its registered effects.

This is an early architecture for agents that can modify and repair, their own harness.

items.title: DeepSeek just did it again.
items.author: Hasan Toor
items.content_text:
DeepSeek just did it again.

They open-sourced their own agent harness that goes straight against Claude Code and Codex.

Every coding harness today ships as a monolith. The prompt, the tools, the memory, the UI, all baked into a single binary.

If you want to swap the model router or add a new tool, you're patching someone else's core. And when the maintainer changes the architecture, your fork breaks.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh) inverts that. The core is tiny. Every capability loads at runtime as a plugin.

Model connectors, tool schemas, the memory layer, and the web UI, all pluggable.

It's built on Cordis, a runtime described in a paper called "A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability."

Plugins load, swap, and unload while the agent is running. No restart.

The repo ships with .claude, .agents, CLAUDE .md, and AGENTS .md folders. That's aimed squarely at anyone stuck inside Anthropic or OpenAI's harness who wants a way out.

items.title: DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepSeek Harness.
items.author: Akshay
items.content_text:
DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepSeek Harness.

(crossed 35k stars in a few hours)

it is built around one core idea: everything is a plugin

let me explain what that means:

the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself are all plugins in DeepSeek Harness (dsh). every one of them can be swapped for your own.

that matters because changing how an agent assembles context usually means editing the framework's own source, or forking it and paying for that fork on every upgrade.

the mechanics that make it work:

→ a plugin claims a stable key like ctx .tools or ctx .llm, and other plugins find it by that key instead of importing a concrete implementation.

→ dependencies are declared rather than hand-sequenced, so load order falls out of what each plugin requires.

→ registrations are reversible, so unloading a plugin unwinds everything it registered.

→ one event, agent/pre-step, decides what the model sees. listeners can rewrite the claimed messages or reject them, which is where nearly all custom context engineering would land.

→ the session log is append-only and covers system prompts, reasoning, tool calls, subagent scheduling, and every context injection.

that last one is what i would actually reach for.

logging tool calls is standard, and when an agent misbehaves you are still guessing at what was in the window. here, model-visible means logged, asserted at runtime, so a new model-visible input requires a new session event.

deepseek was the last major lab shipping coding-grade models without a first-party harness to train against, and it now ships one that can delegate subagent work to Claude Code and Codex.

link to GitHub repo: 
https://
github.com/deepseek-ai/de
epseek-harness
…

if you want the full anatomy of what a harness actually contains, the article is quoted below.
